You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

Diagnosis:
The test method testFloatValueForLargeNumeratorAndDenominator creates very large BigInteger values (with 400 and 401 digits) for the numerator and denominator respectively, and constructs a BigFraction object from them. It then asserts that the floatValue method of BigFraction returns approximately 5 for that fraction.

From the code snippets of BigFraction.doubleValue() and BigFraction.floatValue(), both methods implement the conversion by straightforwardly calling numerator.doubleValue() / denominator.doubleValue() or numerator.floatValue() / denominator.floatValue().

The issue report explains that BigInteger.doubleValue() fails when called on very large BigIntegers that exceed Double.MAX_VALUE, returning NaN or inaccurate results. This is because doubleValue on BigInteger doesn't throw errors but can silently degrade precision or overflow to special double values such as NaN or infinity.

Since the test uses numerators and denominators with hundreds of digits (far above the largest double), the direct calls to BigInteger.doubleValue() or floatValue() in the divisor produce NaN or inaccurate results. Consequently, the division results in NaN or an incorrect float value instead of the expected value (5 in this test).

Therefore, the root cause is that BigFraction.doubleValue() and BigFraction.floatValue() rely directly on numerator.doubleValue() and denominator.doubleValue() which cannot handle very large BigInteger values properly, resulting in inaccurate or NaN output when numerator or denominator are extremely large.

To fix this, the conversion methods need to implement logic to scale down (shift) numerator and denominator before division to bring them safely within the range of doubles, avoiding overflow and preserving accuracy.

Recent issue reports do not seem relevant to this problem, as their topics are unrelated.

In summary:
- Failing test constructs extremely large numerator/denominator BigIntegers.
- BigFraction.doubleValue()/floatValue() directly call BigInteger.doubleValue()/floatValue() on numerator and denominator.
- BigInteger.doubleValue()/floatValue() fail or produce NaN when BigInteger is extremely large.
- Resulting value in BigFraction.doubleValue/floatValue is NaN or inaccurate.
- Need logic in BigFraction to scale numerator and denominator before division to avoid overflow.

This matches the symptom described in the bug report, confirming the diagnosis.

Next, locating the method(s) where the fix should occur would be in BigFraction.doubleValue() and BigFraction.floatValue() methods.
Title: Diagnosis
Details: The failing test tries to compute the floatValue of a BigFraction composed of very large BigInteger numerator and denominator (hundreds of digits). The current implementation of BigFraction.floatValue() (and similarly doubleValue()) simply calls numerator.floatValue() / denominator.floatValue(). According to the bug report, BigInteger.floatValue() (and doubleValue()) cannot handle values larger than Double.MAX_VALUE properly, returning NaN or incorrect results. Since the numerator and denominator are extremely large, their floatValue() conversions fail, causing the fraction's floatValue to be NaN or incorrect. The root cause is that BigFraction.floatValue() and doubleValue() do not handle large BigInteger values safely—they rely on direct doubleValue() / floatValue() calls on BigInteger, which overflow. The fix needs to apply scaling logic in these methods to shift numerator and denominator to a range fitting in double/float before dividing, preserving accuracy and avoiding NaN. Recent reports are unrelated, so the main fault lies in BigFraction.floatValue() and BigFraction.doubleValue() implementations.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
